title: The Long Discourses, closed
hook: from a net that catches every view to a young man bowing in the street

segments.voice: Yesterday: Digha Nikaya, and your line, yours. Did you tell someone your scene? Keep it close. Today we close the whole collection and look at the road it took. Day five hundred seventy-five.

The first long discourse begins on a road. The Buddha and his monks are walking between two cities, and behind them walk a wandering teacher and his student, arguing. The teacher criticizes the Buddha the whole way. The student praises him the whole way. Early next morning the monks are buzzing about it, and the Buddha's first words in the whole collection are about that: if people speak against me, or against the teaching, don't get angry. If they praise us, don't get puffed up. Just say what's true and what isn't. Fifty-odd days later, we've reached the end of that road. Today: the Long Discourses, closed.
screen: `TWO TRAVELERS ARGUING BEHIND.` → `NOT ANGRY, NOT PUFFED UP.` → `THE END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of the journey. It starts huge. In that first discourse, the Buddha lays out sixty-two views about the self and the world, and says every such theory is caught among them, like fish in a fine net cast over a small pond. Every one of them, he says, grows out of feeling and craving. It's a teaching about how minds build positions. Then come the kings, the wanderers and the gods, and the long, slow walk of the last journey to the final words. And then, after all that, the collection comes down to earth. A young man named Sigala in the street at dawn, bowing to the directions because his father asked him to. The Buddha doesn't tell him to stop. He tells him what each bow could mean: parents, teachers, spouse, friends, workers, spiritual teachers. Six ways money leaks. How to know a real friend. And after the four kings' protective verses, it closes with Sariputta, counting the teaching aloud so it stays whole. From the net of every view to how you treat the person who cleans your house. That's the long way home: the biggest questions end up at the kitchen table. Tomorrow a new collection begins, much shorter, with poems some scholars count among the oldest Buddhist verses.
screen: `SIXTY-TWO VIEWS CAUGHT IN A NET` · `KINGS, GODS AND THE LAST JOURNEY` · `SIGALA BOWING IN THE STREET` · `FROM EVERY VIEW TO THE KITCHEN TABLE` · then, large: `THE LONG WAY HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall one long discourse from start to finish. Sit and settle. Pick one, perhaps not yesterday's scene: the moonlit king, the last journey, Sigala's six directions, whichever comes. Tell it to yourself in three beats. How it starts. What turns. How it ends. Slowly, as if you were telling a child at bedtime. If a gap appears, don't worry; just notice the gap and go on. Then let the story go quiet and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
brahmajala. Thirty-four teachings, the Digha Nikaya, running from a net that catches every view to the duties of ordinary life. Today's word.
Your line: the long way home. When a big question fills your head today, bring it home: what would it mean for the next person you'll actually see? Day five hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries the Digha Nikaya is studied, and some of its discourses, such as the advice to Sigala, are taught to lay people as a guide for daily life.

fork.setup: you're one of the monks. all day a wandering teacher has criticized the Buddha on the road. that evening, what does the Buddha tell you?
options: don't be angry or elated; say what's true and what isn't.
fork.reveal: the first long discourse opens with this: neither anger at blame nor pride at praise, only a calm account of what's true.

original.note: Pali brahmajala: the supreme net, the name of DN 1, which catches sixty-two views.

trapdoor: what you thought: the long discourses are a collection of long lectures.
what it means: they travel from the net of every view, through kings, gods and the last journey, to the duties of daily life.
what a scholar hears: the Digha Nikaya opens with the Brahmajala Sutta on views and closes with DN 33 and 34, Sariputta's lists, after the lay ethics of DN 31.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta: praise and blame; the net of sixty-two views

notes: Block close for the Long Discourses (days 522–575). Confirm the DN 1 opening: the wanderer Suppiya criticizing and his student Brahmadatta praising, on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda.
Confirm that the sixty-two views are traced to feeling and craving in DN 1.
The order of DN 31–34 in the canon: DN 31 (Sigalovada), DN 32 (Atanatiya), DN 33, DN 34. The script says the collection 'closes with Sariputta' after Sigala; DN 32 sits between them.

Editor review (y2 557-575): DN 1's monks discuss the wanderers at dawn the next morning, not 'that evening'; the net of views now says what DN 1 says (every such theory falls within the sixty-two) rather than 'every theory people of his day held'; trimmed the scene-by-scene recap that repeated day 574 almost item for item; DN 32 is acknowledged before Sariputta's closing lists; tomorrow's 'oldest words' is attributed to some scholars; unverified 'festivals and memorials' cut from howItsDone.
